extracted.intended_audience: European Commission staff (DG evaluators, impact assessment authors, policy leads), RSB members, and other Commission services involved in evaluations, impact assessments and implementation strategies
extracted.subtask_short: EU evaluation and impact assessment reports
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, conducting and reporting evaluation and impact assessment work for European Commission initiatives, including procedural steps, quality principles, required content and publication/transmission rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness (evaluation criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: evaluations should cover at least the following criteria: effectiveness; efficiency; relevance; coherence; and EU added value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other criteria may be added as appropriate. The evidence gathered on the targeted questions addressing each of the five evaluation criteria should feed into the analytical narrative and may be documented in Annex III (evaluation matrix and answers to the evaluation questions (by evaluation criterion)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality (evaluation scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: the scope of the evaluation must be tailored to the particular intervention, the time since its implementation and the available data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some criteria new data will need to be collected, analysed and compared; for others a short summary based on existing reports or a standard explanation may be acceptable. In general, do not conduct an evaluation until you have at least 3 years of reasonably full implementation data where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and objectivity (evaluation conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: only independent and objective evaluations can deliver robust and reliable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An analysis can be considered independent/objective (even if based on a contractor study) provided it is based on all relevant information, conducted without influence or pressure by third parties, and reports transparently on positive and negative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based approach
rubrics_metrics.description: evaluations should be based on the best available evidence drawn from a diverse and appropriate range of methods and sources (triangulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all sources are equally robust; consider when/how evidence was collected and whether it is subject to bias or uncertainty. Where necessary conduct sensitivity and/or scenario analysis. Any limitations related to evidence and methodology must be clearly explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: evaluations must make judgments on the basis of the available evidence and analysis; judgments should be as specific as possible and judgment criteria should be identified in the evaluation design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative should clearly present arguments supporting judgments and reference which evaluation criterion they relate to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — expected outcome / intervention logic
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the expected outcome of the intervention? The evaluation should explain the rationale for the intervention at the time it was prepared/adopted (problem, underlying causes, expected achievements and how achievement was to be assessed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on the impact assessment, explanatory memorandum and preamble of the legal text where possible and include points of comparison and references to relevant SDGs the intervention aimed to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — evolution over evaluation period
rubrics_metrics.description: How has the situation evolved over the evaluation period? The evaluation gives a factual presentation of progress in implementing the intervention (both legally and on the ground).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factual evidence of implementation and changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — success (effectiveness, efficiency, coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent was the intervention successful and why? Success is assessed in terms of the extent to which an intervention achieves its objectives: effectively, efficiently and in a coherent way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare expected vs actual situation; present quantitative terms of benefits and costs where possible; analysis of efficiency should cover administrative and adjustment costs and simplification potential. Outline costs and benefits in Annex IV 'Overview of benefits and costs' and, where relevant, a separate 'Simplification and burden reduction' table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — EU added value
rubrics_metrics.description: How did the EU intervention make a difference? The evaluation should give an assessment of the intervention’s EU added value for individuals and businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond restating legal objectives to present an ex post evidence-based assessment, explaining clearly to whom the EU intervention made a difference and, where relevant, provide territorial breakdowns (rural, urban, cross-border, outermost regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation question — relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the intervention still relevant? The evaluation should assess how well objectives reflected and still reflect current and future needs (continuing relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight mismatches between original objectives and current/future needs, consider strategic foresight, and explain reasons for mismatches to inform decisions to maintain, adjust or terminate the intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions and lessons learned (evaluation outputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should present conclusions including which elements of the intervention are (not) working and why, a summary of benefits that could not have been achieved without EU involvement, and credible evidence-based lessons and areas for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include lessons relating to REFIT issues: regulatory or unnecessary burden, simplicity/complexity, efficiencies/inefficiencies and achievement of objectives at appropriate cost; explore environmental and digital transition implications where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation report quality and format
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation report must answer the prescribed evaluation questions, explain method, evidence base and analysis, and be a transparent, objective and balanced presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report should be concise (not longer than 50 pages of text), non-technical (accessible to non-experts), self-standing (sufficient detail to follow evidence and logic), include a synopsis report annex summarising stakeholder views, systematically reference all external material, and use Annexes (III, IV) for detailed matrices and costs/benefits. Where no submission to EP/Council is required prepare short executive summary (max 4–5 DGT pages) in English, French and German.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interservice group involvement (evaluations and impact assessments)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interservice group should be set up and involved in all key steps of the evaluation/impact assessment following validation, up to launch of interservice consultation and related communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a public consultation is conducted the interservice group should be involved in preparing the questionnaire. The interservice group should help identify relevant and significant impacts for evidence collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Regulatory Scrutiny Board (RSB)
rubrics_metrics.description: For selected evaluations and all fitness checks the draft report must be submitted to the RSB and the interservice consultation cannot be launched before the RSB has issued its opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RSB will scrutinise draft reports and issue opinions and recommendations. If the opinion is negative the lead DG(s) may submit a revised draft for a second opinion but are not obliged to. For impact assessments a positive RSB opinion is required before proceeding to interservice consultation; two negative opinions require the vice-president for better regulation to give the green light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and transparency obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximise transparency, the final evaluation/impact assessment report alongside the 'call for evidence', related consultation documents, contractor's final study (if applicable) and the RSB opinion must be published centrally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials must be published on the 'Have Your Say' web portal; contractor studies are published on the DG's website. Impact assessment reports are published on the Register of Commission Documents and 'Have Your Say' and transmitted to the legislator with supporting documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding evaluation results into governance
rubrics_metrics.description: DGs must feed evaluation results into their annual activity reports and identify follow-up actions in their annual management plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and sharing planned follow-up actions is part of accepting responsibility and accountability and ensures transparency; findings should stimulate discussion and inform follow-up action such as an impact assessment, improved guidance or further monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an impact assessment is required
rubrics_metrics.description: An impact assessment is required for Commission initiatives likely to have significant economic, environmental or social impacts, which entail significant spending, and where the Commission has a choice of policy options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All spending programmes, financial instruments and budgetary guarantees entailing significant expenditure (indicatively > EUR 5 million) should be accompanied by an ex ante evaluation (financial statement). Where an impact assessment is required in principle but a derogation is granted, prepare an analytical staff working document within three months of adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact assessments must be comprehensive, proportionate, evidence-based, open to stakeholders' views, unbiased, prepared collectively with relevant services, embedded in the policy cycle, transparent and of high quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles guide the choice of methods, depth of analysis and presentation of results; strategic foresight and independent scientific advice may be used where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment questions (Box 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: An impact assessment should answer: (1) What is the problem and why is it a problem? (2) Why should the EU act? (3) What should be achieved? (4) What are the options for achieving the objectives? (5) What are their economic, social and environmental impacts and who will be affected? (6) How do the options compare (effectiveness, efficiency and coherence)? (7) How will monitoring and subsequent evaluation be organised?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers should consider dynamic baselines, long-term trends, SDGs, impacts on SMEs, gender, territories, fundamental rights, 'do no significant harm' and 'digital by default' principles, and support decision-making by identifying preferred options where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment methodological guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Select appropriate methods to collect/interpret data and analyse impacts; assess all relevant impacts qualitatively and quantitatively where possible; make systematic efforts to quantify impacts proportionately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use results of evaluations and fitness checks as starting points; commission external studies or scientific advice where necessary; include simulation models in MIDAS when used; assess impacts relative to a dynamic baseline; discount monetised estimates as appropriate; assess distributional and cumulative burdens and explain limitations/uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment report content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The final impact assessment report must be transparent, objective and balanced, written for non-expert readers, self-standing and limited to 40 pages of text with annexes as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report must contain at least: description of social, economic and environmental impacts (and explicit statement if any are not significant); clear indication of who will be affected and how with quantification of costs/benefits; impacts on fundamental rights; impacts on SMEs and competitiveness; consideration of 'do no significant harm' and 'digital by default' principles; consistency with European Climate Law; assessment of impacts on relevant SDGs; detailed consultation strategy and synopsis report annex. Prepare an executive summary (4–5 DGT pages) as a separate linked staff working document translated into all EU official languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: From impact assessment to policymaking — explanatory memorandum items
rubrics_metrics.description: The explanatory memorandum accompanying proposals should cover legal basis, subsidiarity, proportionality, results of evaluations and fitness checks, results of stakeholder consultations, a short summary of input from external experts, and a summary of the impact assessment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also cover consultation of the RSB, regulatory fitness and simplification, conformity with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, description of main impact categories, conformity with 'do no significant harm' and 'digital by default', contribution to relevant SDGs, and description of monitoring/evaluation/reporting arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prepare an implementation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation strategies should be prepared for all major directives and regulations to track progress in implementation and the subsequent collection/use of data for reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normally not required for acts that already include provisions for tracking implementation, have a limited/very technical scope, impose only one or very few legal obligations, or amend only one or very few existing obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation strategy content
rubrics_metrics.description: The implementation strategy should include all major steps the Commission should take when monitoring compliance of national laws with EU legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular it should identify the various types of support the Commission services will provide to assist Member States in transposition/implementation and set out arrangements for monitoring implementation, including a timeline for compliance assessments, possible enforcement action and implementation reports.
